questions.enonce_markdown:
Explain **Four (4)** determinants of the size of the national income.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** *National income* is the total value of goods and services produced by the citizens of a country in a year, together with income from abroad. The following factors determine its size.

1. **Quantity and quality of natural resources.** A country with fertile land, forests, minerals and oil can produce more than one that is poor in resources, provided that the resources are exploited.
2. **Size and quality of the labour force.** A large, healthy, educated and skilled working population produces more. Training and good health raise the productivity of labour and therefore the national income.
3. **Capital stock and level of investment.** Machines, factories, roads, electricity and other capital goods increase production per worker. The more a country saves and invests, the faster its output and its national income grow.
4. **State of technology.** Better methods of production (improved seeds, machines, computers) allow more output from the same resources.
5. **Political stability, good government and a good business climate.** Peace, security, law and order and sound policies encourage investment and production; war, corruption and instability destroy them.
6. **Size of the market and foreign trade.** Large demand at home and abroad encourages firms to produce more.

*Any four, each explained.*

**Conclusion.** National income is determined by the quantity and quality of the factors of production and by the conditions in which they are used.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Explain **Three (3)** problems encountered when measuring national income.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** National income is calculated by the output, income or expenditure methods, but several problems make the figure inaccurate.

1. **Double counting.** The same output may be counted more than once, for example when the value of cocoa is counted, then again in the value of the chocolate made from it. Only the value of **final goods** or the **value added** at each stage should be counted, and this requires careful data.
2. **Non-marketed and subsistence production.** Many goods and services are not sold in the market and so are not recorded: food grown and consumed by farm families, housework and services done at home or between neighbours. National income in developing countries is therefore under-estimated.
3. **Hidden (black) economy and tax evasion.** Illegal activities and the many small businesses that are not registered or that hide their income to avoid taxes are left out of the official statistics, so the figures are too low.
4. **Inflation (changes in the price level).** A rise in national income in money terms may be due to higher prices and not to higher output, so real national income must be calculated with a price index.
5. **Lack of reliable data.** Illiteracy, poor record-keeping, shortage of trained statisticians and the scattered location of producers make the data inaccurate and incomplete.

*Any three, each explained.*

**Conclusion.** Because of these problems, national income statistics are estimates and must be used with caution when comparing countries or years.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Briefly explain the following:

(i) Consumption.

(ii) Investment.

(iii) Gross Domestic Product.

(2+2+2=6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Consumption** is the spending by households on goods and services (food, clothes, rent, transport, school fees...) to satisfy their wants during a period. It is the largest component of total spending in most economies.

**(ii) Investment** is the spending by firms (and by the government) on **capital goods** such as machines, factories, buildings, roads and stocks, in order to increase the capacity to produce in the future. It is an addition to the capital stock of the country; buying existing shares or land is not investment in this economic sense.

**(iii) Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** is the total market value of all **final goods and services produced within the geographical boundaries of a country in one year**, whether the producers are citizens or foreigners, before deducting depreciation (capital consumption).
